extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, empirical researchers, patent litigators, and policymakers studying patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_short: empirical analysis of patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: An empirical study measuring outcomes of patent litigation (invalidity and infringement) across technologies and industries, using summary judgment, trial, and appellate decisions and multivariate logistic regressions to identify correlates of patentee success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity-102 Prior Art (102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity under 35 U.S.C. §102 (prior art) — recorded as “Invalidity-102 Prior Art-All--Any stage” in the tables and analyzed by technology and industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports frequency and percent of successful 102 challenges by technology and industry, notes that technology differences were statistically significant (though 'barely above the 95% confidence threshold' for 102 in one comparison), and provides Pearson chi-squared tests for cross-category differences (see Table results). Use of 102 is treated as one distinct ground for invalidity in outcome analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity-103 Obviousness (103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity based on 35 U.S.C. §103 (obviousness) — recorded as “Invalidity-103-Obviousness--Any Stage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports success rates on obviousness challenges by technology and industry (percent ranges and frequencies), highlights substantial cross-industry and cross-technology variation (e.g., range from 0% to 77.8% by industry), and reports Pearson chi-squared significance (p=0.000 in many comparisons). Small cell sizes are noted as a caveat when interpreting extreme percentages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity-112 Indefiniteness (section 112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity on grounds of indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) — recorded as “Invalidity-112-Indefiniteness--Any Stage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper documents that indefiniteness arguments succeeded at very different rates across technologies (e.g., nearly a quarter in software, a third in electronics, 0% in mechanical and biotech, ~3% in chemicals). It links higher indefiniteness success in software to particular definiteness rules that apply to means-plus-function claims and summarizes case law requiring disclosure of corresponding algorithms (Aristocrat, Function Media, ePlus, Ergo, Noah Systems, In re Aoyama, Typhoon Touch, Dell). The authors caution small sample sizes in some categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity-112 Inadequate Disclosure (enablement / written description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity under section 112 as inadequate disclosure (enablement and written description) — recorded as “Invalidity-112-Inadequate Disclosure--Any stage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported success rates vary by technology (e.g., one third of mechanical decisions and three-quarters of biotechnology decisions on these grounds resulted in invalidity; much lower rates in software and electronics). The paper treats enablement/written-description challenges separately from indefiniteness and highlights statistical significance (p=0.008 for disclosure comparisons) while warning about small Ns in some cells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome classification: definitive win vs procedural posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of outcomes distinguishing definitive wins (e.g., defendant summary judgment of invalidity as a case win) from non-definitive procedural events (e.g., patentee defeating summary judgment on an issue but not obtaining a case win).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that a defendant who wins summary judgment of invalidity is a definitive winner for purposes of certain tables, whereas a patentee who merely defeats a motion for summary judgment on an issue may appear as a 'winner' in some tables but not in overall definitive-win tallies. Procedural posture categories include summary judgment, trial (jury/judge), and appeals; some analyses condition on final determinations of validity or infringement disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome metrics: patentee win rate, invalidity rate, infringement findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary outcome measures used: overall patentee win rate (definitive winner), invalidity rate (accused infringer success on invalidity), and findings of infringement (direct literal + doctrine of equivalents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results are reported by technology and industry (tables and figures), with frequencies, percentages, and chi-squared tests. Separate tables break down invalidity and infringement outcomes by industry (Tables 8–11, Figures 6–8). The paper emphasizes that percentages alone can be misleading when the number of observed motions/cases differs across categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and industry categorical variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of technology-area categories (mechanics, electronics, chemistry, biotech, software, optics, etc.) and industry categories (pharmaceuticals, medical devices, computer & electronics, communications, consumer goods, transportation, construction, energy, industrial/business goods) as explanatory variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper distinguishes technology (the nature of the claimed technology) from industry (the industry deploying the patent) and presents outcomes by both. The analyses show significant differences across both axes and argue for interpreting technology- and industry-specific patterns separately (e.g., biotech technology vs biotech industry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent and lawsuit covariates included in regressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent and litigation characteristics included as covariates in multivariate regressions: inventor domestic/foreign status, number of claims, number of prior art references cited, number of other patents that cite this patent, patent age at filing of suit (how old when suit filed), number of defendants sued, and number of other patents asserted in the same case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These variables were incorporated alongside technology and industry dummies in logistic regression specifications to control for patent and lawsuit heterogeneity. The paper reports multiple specifications (primary and alternative), and notes internal consistency across specifications. Appendices present full specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methodology: bootstrapping, clustering, and model choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of bootstrapping to control false discovery rate, clustering of standard errors on unique patent numbers to address non-independence, and running separate logistic regressions for each merits outcome (rather than a multinomial model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bootstrapping procedure: resample the original data to construct fifty samples of the original size (e.g., 949 observations), run the logistic regression on each random sample to generate coefficients and standard errors, add each random sample back into the data iteratively, average the fifty coefficients, and derive final standard errors and p-values. Standard errors were clustered on unique patent numbers in each bootstrap regression. Separate logits were required because different outcomes per patent were not independent, preventing a single multinomial specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: District effects and regression specification limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of district-of-filing dummies in some regression specifications to control for judicial/regional effects, with constraints due to degrees-of-freedom limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors ran specifications controlling for district (Appendix B) and truncated sets of district dummies representing the top districts (Appendix C); an omnibus model included only three important districts (E.D. Tex, D. Del., N.D. Cal.) because of degrees-of-freedom limitations. The paper highlights significant district-level associations (e.g., Eastern District of Texas more likely to rule for patentees) and discusses procedural practices (judges requiring permission to file summary judgment) that may affect observed rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation caveats: small sample sizes, selection, and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cautions about small numbers in some categories, potential selection bias, and the non-representativeness of litigated-and-adjudicated patents versus all patents (or even all litigated patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors repeatedly warn that small cell counts can make percentages sensitive to a few cases (e.g., biotech small N), note that their dataset includes only a subset of filed suits (less than 10% of filed lawsuits in study years) and largely excludes settled cases (whose terms are confidential), and outline a 'selection story' whereby patents reaching judgment may not be representative of all patents. These caveats qualify causal or general claims from the observed associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function doctrine effect on software claim definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal rule: means-plus-function software claims require disclosure of the corresponding algorithm in the specification, failing which the claim can be invalid as indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper cites a line of Federal Circuit cases (Aristocrat, Function Media, ePlus, Ergo, Noah Systems, In re Aoyama, Typhoon Touch v. Dell) illustrating that algorithms must be disclosed for means-plus-function claims; this doctrinal feature likely contributes to higher indefiniteness success rates in software cases in the dataset. The authors note that many patents in the dataset were drafted before development of this case law, possibly explaining failures on indefiniteness grounds.
